analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at ten percentage points above the prime rate.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card interest rates died in committee without a hearing or vote, having attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a ceiling into federal law on the interest rate credit card companies can charge: no more than ten percentage points above the prime rate, the benchmark rate banks use, updated each quarter. When the bill was introduced in September 2004, the prime rate was under 5%, so the ceiling would have been roughly 15% — well below the rates many cardholders were paying. The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Cardholders carrying balances at high interest rates. A cap tied to the prime rate would have limited how much credit card companies could charge on unpaid balances, reducing finance charges for the millions of households who carry credit card debt month to month.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amended the Truth in Lending Act to bar a creditor from charging a credit card annual percentage rate greater than ten percentage points over the most recent composite prime rate published in the Wall Street Journal, updated each quarter.
With the prime rate below 5% in late 2004, the ceiling would have been roughly 15% — lower than the rates on many credit cards, so cardholders carrying balances would pay less in interest each month.
The Federal Reserve Board would have been authorized to issue regulations to implement the rate ceiling and publish the maximum allowed rate each quarter.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that earn revenue from finance charges on revolving balances. Issuers could also have responded by tightening credit standards or shifting costs into fees, which would fall on borrowers with weaker credit.

drawbacks.text: A hard rate cap can shrink access to credit: lenders who cannot price a borrower's risk through interest would rationally lend less or not at all to higher-risk customers, and could recover revenue through fees instead, which fall hardest on people who pay late or carry balances.

The cap was pegged to a floating benchmark, so when prime rates rise the ceiling rises with them, meaning cardholders would not be protected from higher rates in a rising-rate environment — only from spreads above prime plus ten points.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A rate ceiling near 15% would have delivered real savings to households carrying high-rate card debt, which is the largest group of credit card users by balance. The main cost is that some higher-risk borrowers might have lost access to credit cards or paid more in fees as lenders adjusted. Whether that tradeoff is worth it is a genuine policy judgment, but the bill never received a hearing or analysis in committee, so the merits were never debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2004, referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2005 — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Bell introduced the Fair Credit Card Interest Rate Act on September 23, 2004, in the final weeks of the 108th Congress.

The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee, and two weeks later to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where subcommittee referral is typically where a bill without leadership support goes to stall.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and no committee action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so it never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and banks are better off, since they kept charging interest rates above what the proposed prime-plus-ten ceiling would have allowed, with no debate or vote on the merits.

for.name: Rep. Chris Bell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it with no cosponsors; it died in committee two weeks into its life.

against.name: Rep. Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to a subcommittee and received no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: The bill would have capped the finance charges that are the core revenue on revolving card balances, limiting rates to prime plus ten points. Issuers kept the ability to charge higher spreads when the bill died without a vote.
